# How `async` and `defer` work on `<script>`

## The default case: no attribute

A classic `<script src="…">` with neither attribute stops the parser. The browser fetches and runs the script, and only then continues parsing the page. The WHATWG spec says such a script is "fetched and evaluated immediately, blocking parsing until these are both complete" (https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/scripting.html). web.dev says the same, adding that rendering is blocked too (https://web.dev/learn/performance/optimize-resource-loading). Because the parser waits for these scripts, they always run before DOMContentLoaded (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Document/DOMContentLoaded_event).

## `async` on a classic external script

**Parsing.** The script downloads while parsing continues. The spec says it is evaluated "as soon as it is available (potentially before parsing completes)" (https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/scripting.html). So an async script does not block parsing while it downloads. If it finishes downloading while the parser is still working, it interrupts the parser to run (https://web.dev/articles/efficiently-load-third-party-javascript).

**Timing relative to DOMContentLoaded.** DOMContentLoaded does not wait for async scripts (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Document/DOMContentLoaded_event). An async script can therefore run either before or after the event, depending on when it finishes downloading. The sources do not fully agree on this:
- One sentence on MDN's DOMContentLoaded page says the event fires "before the execution of scripts with async".
- Elsewhere on that same page, MDN treats `<script async>` as something that *may* run after DOMContentLoaded.
- web.dev and the spec both say an async script can run while parsing is still under way. Since DOMContentLoaded comes after parsing ends, that would put the script before the event.

My reading is that "before or after" is correct and that MDN's one-line note oversimplifies. That is an inference. None of the workers could confirm it from the spec's end-of-parsing steps, because https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/parsing.html returned HTTP 404.

**Order.** There is no ordering guarantee. In the spec, async scripts go into an unordered "set of scripts that will execute as soon as possible", and each runs when its own download is ready. In practice, whichever script loads first runs first. web.dev calls out-of-order execution "possible (and likely)".

## `defer` on a classic external script

**Parsing.** The script is fetched in parallel with parsing and never blocks the parser. The spec says it is evaluated "when the page has finished parsing" (https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/scripting.html).

**Timing relative to DOMContentLoaded.** Deferred scripts run after parsing finishes but before DOMContentLoaded, and the event waits for them. MDN describes the order this way:
- `document.readyState` becomes "interactive".
- The deferred scripts run.
- DOMContentLoaded fires.

Deferred scripts also wait for stylesheets (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Document/DOMContentLoaded_event). One web.dev page loosely says this happens "at the same time as" DOMContentLoaded. A second web.dev page, and MDN, say "before", which is the more precise wording.

**Order.** Deferred scripts run in document order (MDN, web.dev). The spec appends each parser-inserted deferred script to the end of a list that runs once parsing finishes. The text the worker read did not state the run order in so many words, so for the spec this is a reasonable inference rather than a confirmed quote.

## Both attributes on one script

`async` wins: the script behaves as if only `async` were set. `defer` is only there so that old browsers which support `defer` but not `async` use deferred loading instead of blocking (spec, MDN).

## Inline scripts (no `src`)

For classic inline scripts, `async` and `defer` have no effect. The spec only applies the async/defer branching when the script is classic with a `src` attribute, or is a module script. MDN warns against using either attribute on inline classic scripts for this reason. An inline classic script runs immediately and blocks the parser (MDN, web.dev).

## `type="module"` scripts

**Deferred by default.** Module scripts behave like deferred scripts even without the attribute, so adding `defer` changes nothing. The spec says "The defer attribute has no effect on module scripts", and MDN says the same. According to web.dev, automatic deferral applies to inline module scripts as well.

**Timing.** DOMContentLoaded waits for non-async module scripts in the same way it waits for `defer` scripts (MDN).

**With `async`.** Adding `async` changes how a module script runs. The script and all its dependencies are fetched in parallel with parsing, and the module runs as soon as everything is available, with no ordering guarantee.

**Two points the workers did not confirm directly:**
- No source they opened explicitly says that non-async modules keep document order. That conclusion combines two MDN statements: modules "defer by default", and deferred scripts run in document order.
- No source explicitly says that `async` works on *inline* module scripts. MDN limits its "no effect on inline scripts" warning to classic scripts, which implies it does work, and the spec's branching includes all module scripts.

## Gaps in the research

- The spec's parsing page and the javascript.info articles both returned 404, so they are not cited.
